idiom_name: func(<-chan T) <-chan U stages, close() as EOF, context for cancellation
implementation_notes: A Go pipeline is a series of stages where each stage is a goroutine (or a group of them) that receives values from an inbound channel, transforms them and sends them on an outbound channel - the channel is the pipe, its buffer is the backpressure knob, and closing the outbound channel signals EOF to the next stage. The stage interface is just func(<-chan T) <-chan U, so the classic Filter and Pipe classes never appear; fan-out (several goroutines on one channel) and fan-in (merge) add throughput inside a stage. Cancellation must be explicit: pass a context or a done channel and select on it, because a downstream stage that stops receiving otherwise leaks the upstream goroutines.
pitfalls: Every stage that returns before draining its inbound channel leaks the upstream goroutines (they block on send forever); use a done channel or context cancellation and close your own outbound channel.
Unbuffered channels make each stage wait on its slowest neighbour while a guessed buffer size only hides the bottleneck - measure before choosing a capacity.
Only the sender should close a channel; closing from the consumer side, or closing twice, panics the pipeline.

variants.name: io.Reader/io.Writer middleware chain
variants.idiom_name: func(io.Writer) io.Writer filter decorators with io.Copy and io.Pipe
variants.implementation_notes: The byte-stream form keeps the pattern's roles as interface values instead of channels: a filter wraps an io.Writer (or is an io.Reader), stages are composed by nesting them, io.Copy pumps the records and io.Pipe() connects a stage running in its own goroutine, which is how the standard library's own filters (bufio, gzip, base64) compose. Choose it when reuse of stdlib codecs matters or the payload is an undelimited byte stream; channels fit better when records are structured values and stages should run concurrently.
pitfalls: io.Writer's contract requires consuming all supplied bytes or returning an error; silently accepting a partial write corrupts the stream for every later stage.
io.Pipe is synchronous: each Write blocks until a Read consumes it, so a stage that never closes its writer (or never reads) hangs its partner - use CloseWithError to propagate failures.
Wrapping writers without flushing (bufio) loses buffered tails when the program exits; a write-through stage must flush before finishing.
